meta.titre: Computer Generations: identifying a generation from its technology and explaining what each one brought
meta.sous_theme: Technology, features and limits of each generation

sections.contenu_markdown: Picture a visitor to a computer museum who sees a room-sized machine full of glass tubes and, beside it, a pocket calculator, and asks how both can be called computers. The answer is the story of the generations of computers: each generation is defined by the main electronic technology used to build the processor, and each brought machines that were smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable. GCE questions ask you to recognise a generation from its technology, to give characteristics of two generations, and to explain what makes a modern laptop powerful.

items: A computer processes data under the control of a stored program.
Hardware is the physical parts of a computer and software is the programs that run on it.
A machine language is made of binary instructions that the processor executes directly.

sections.titre: The five generations and what defines each one
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Principle
Computers are grouped into **generations** according to the main technology of their electronic circuits. The dates below are approximate and textbooks differ by a few years, so identify a generation by its technology first.

| Generation | Main technology | Characteristics |
|---|---|---|
| First (about 1940s to mid 1950s) | vacuum tubes | very large, high electricity use, much heat, frequent failures; programmed in machine language; punched cards and magnetic tape |
| Second (about mid 1950s to mid 1960s) | transistors | smaller, faster, cheaper, cooler and more reliable; assembly language and early high-level languages such as FORTRAN and COBOL; magnetic core memory |
| Third (about mid 1960s to 1970s) | integrated circuits (many transistors on one silicon chip) | smaller and cheaper again; keyboard and monitor replace punched cards and printouts; operating systems that run several programs; high-level languages |
| Fourth (from the 1970s) | microprocessor (the whole processor on one chip, very large scale integration) | personal computers and laptops; graphical user interfaces; networks; semiconductor memory |
| Fifth (present and developing) | very high levels of integration and parallel processing | aims at artificial intelligence, speech and natural language, knowledge-based systems |

### Why each change mattered
Replacing a component made machines smaller, because the new part is smaller; cooler and cheaper to run, because it uses less power; and more reliable, because it has no heated filament to burn out. Always attach the reason to the improvement.

### The power of a laptop
A modern laptop, for example one with an Intel Core i7 processor, is built around a microprocessor, the defining technology of the fourth generation; some textbooks call present-day machines fifth generation, so justify your choice by the technology. Two characteristics mainly decide the power of a laptop. The **processor** determines how many instructions are carried out per second; it is described by its clock speed in GHz and its number of cores. The **RAM** capacity decides how many programs and how much data can be worked on at once without slowing down. Storage type (a solid-state drive is faster than a hard disk) and graphics also matter, but screen size and brand do not make a laptop more powerful.

variantes.nom: Identify a generation from a description
variantes.quand_utiliser: The question describes a machine and asks for its generation.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Find the defining technology first: tubes mean first generation, discrete transistors second, integrated circuits on boards third, a single-chip microprocessor fourth. Then confirm with the supporting clues (size, language, input and output devices) and name the generation with two reasons.

variantes.quand_utiliser: The question asks for an improvement, a characteristic or a difference.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Compare on the same criteria: component, size, heat and power, reliability, speed, software and cost. Write the criterion, the older generation, the newer generation and the reason. For example: size, vacuum-tube machines filled rooms and transistor machines did not, because a transistor is far smaller than a tube.

sections.enonce_markdown: A museum label reads: "This computer was built from separate transistors mounted on circuit boards. It was programmed in assembly language, stored data on magnetic tape and processed jobs in batches. It was smaller and gave off less heat than the machines before it." (a) Identify its generation, with two reasons. (b) State two improvements over the previous generation, with the cause. (c) Name the technology that replaced its main component and the generation that technology started.

etapes.justification: The generation is fixed by the component used to build the processor.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Separate transistors on boards: the technology of the **second generation**.

etapes.justification: A second clue prevents confusion with a neighbouring generation.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Assembly language (instead of machine language only) and magnetic tape storage with batch processing are typical of the second generation; the first generation used tubes, and the third used integrated circuits.

etapes.action: Give two improvements and their causes.
etapes.justification: An improvement is credited only if the cause is stated.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Smaller and cooler, because a transistor is much smaller than a vacuum tube and has no filament to heat. More reliable, because there is no filament to burn out.

etapes.justification: Each generation ends when its main component is superseded.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The transistor was replaced by the **integrated circuit**, which put many transistors on one chip and started the third generation.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The machine belongs to the **second generation** because its processor uses transistors and it runs assembly-language programs from magnetic tape. It improved on the first generation by being smaller and cooler, since transistors replaced tubes, and more reliable, since there is no filament to fail. The integrated circuit later replaced the discrete transistor and began the third generation.

items.erreur_markdown: Deciding the generation by the appearance or the age of the machine, such as "it is a laptop, so it is third generation".
items.pourquoi_faux: A generation is defined by its main circuit technology, not by shape or date.
items.correction_markdown: Identify the technology (tubes, transistors, integrated circuits, microprocessor) and read the generation from it.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing only "smaller and faster" for an improvement.
items.pourquoi_faux: A bare adjective earns little; the question wants an improvement explained.
items.correction_markdown: Add the cause: "smaller, because a transistor is much smaller than a vacuum tube".

items.erreur_markdown: Confusing the integrated circuit with the microprocessor.
items.pourquoi_faux: An integrated circuit is a chip of many transistors; third generation machines still had a processor built from many such chips. The microprocessor puts the whole processor on one chip.
items.correction_markdown: Integrated circuits mean third generation; a single-chip processor means fourth generation.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that first generation computers used high-level languages and second generation used only machine language.
items.pourquoi_faux: The order is reversed: first generation machines used machine language, and assembly and early high-level languages came with the second.
items.correction_markdown: First: machine language. Second: assembly language and early high-level languages.

items.erreur_markdown: Describing the power of a laptop by its screen size, colour or brand.
items.pourquoi_faux: Power is the ability to process data quickly; it depends on the processor and the memory.
items.correction_markdown: Name the processor (clock speed, cores) and the RAM capacity, and say what each does.

items.enonce_markdown: Match each technology to its generation: (a) integrated circuits, (b) vacuum tubes, (c) microprocessor, (d) transistors.
(a) Give one characteristic of first generation computers and one of fourth generation computers. (b) Explain two reasons why the microprocessor made personal computers possible.
items.solution_markdown: (a) First: very large, used vacuum tubes, produced much heat, programmed in machine language (any one). Fourth: built around a microprocessor, small enough for the desk or the lap, used with graphical interfaces and networks (any one). (b) Award a mark for each reason with its cause: the whole processor sits on one small chip, so the computer can be small; mass production of chips makes the computer cheap enough for individuals and schools; a chip needs little power and gives off little heat, so no special room or cooling is needed.

items.enonce_markdown: A student says: "Each new generation of computers improved on the one before, so the generation of a laptop depends on how much it costs." (a) Explain, with two examples, how later generations improved on earlier ones. (b) Explain why the second part of the statement is wrong. (c) Give the two characteristics that determine the power of a laptop and describe them.
items.solution_markdown: (a) Award a mark for each example with its cause: size, because a transistor is much smaller than a vacuum tube, so machines no longer filled a room; reliability and heat, because transistors and chips have no filament to burn out or heat; cost, because integrated circuits and microprocessors are mass produced. (b) A generation is defined by the technology of the circuits, not by price: a cheap and an expensive laptop are both microprocessor machines. (c) The **processor**: its clock speed in GHz and number of cores set how many instructions are executed per second. The **RAM**: its capacity sets how many programs and how much data can be handled at once.

items_markdown: A generation is defined by the main circuit technology: vacuum tubes, transistors, integrated circuits, microprocessor, then artificial-intelligence goals.
Each change made machines smaller, cooler, cheaper and more reliable; always attach the cause to the improvement.
Machine language belongs to the first generation; assembly and early high-level languages came with the second.
Integrated circuits (many chips on boards) are the third generation; the single-chip microprocessor starts the fourth.
The power of a laptop depends mainly on its processor (clock speed, cores) and its RAM capacity.
